hints: Focus on the attacking species in the equation, it is the free cyanide ion $CN^-$ acting as a nucleophile to replace $Br$.
Consider which reagent actually supplies plenty of free $CN^-$ ions, $KCN$ which fully ionises or $HCN$ which is a very weak acid.
Think about why the solvent must be ethanolic and not dilute sulfuric acid, since acid would remove the nucleophile and hydrolyse the nitrile product.
walkthrough:
**Recognise the reaction type**

Great spot, this is nucleophilic substitution of a halogenoalkane. The $C-Br$ bond is polar, so $CN^-$ attacks the electron-deficient carbon and kicks out $Br^-$.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN} + \text{Br}^-$$

**Choose the source of CN-**

We need a high concentration of the strong nucleophile $CN^-$. Potassium cyanide is ionic and dissolves to give free ions.

$$\text{KCN} \rightarrow \text{K}^+ + \text{CN}^-$$

**Choose the correct conditions**

We heat under reflux in ethanol, not in water or acid. Ethanol dissolves both the organic bromoalkane and the $KCN$, allowing substitution to form the nitrile. Dilute sulfuric acid would protonate $CN^-$ to $HCN$ and would hydrolyse the nitrile product to a carboxylic acid.

options.A: Reagent $KCN$ is correct, but dilute sulfuric acid is wrong. Acid protonates $CN^-$ to form $HCN$ gas ($CN^- + H^+ \rightarrow HCN$), removing the nucleophile, and it would hydrolyse the $CH_3CH_2CH_2CN$ product.
options.B: This is correct. $KCN$ provides free $CN^-$ nucleophiles, and heating under reflux in ethanol provides a suitable solvent that dissolves both reactants and favours nucleophilic substitution to lengthen the chain by one carbon.
options.C: $HCN$ is a very weak acid and gives almost no free $CN^-$, so it is a poor nucleophile source for halogenoalkanes. It is used with $KCN$ catalyst for aldehydes and ketones, not here, and acid conditions are also wrong.
options.D: Ethanolic reflux is the right type of condition, but $HCN$ is the wrong reagent. Without $K^+$ salt ionisation there are too few $CN^-$ ions for effective substitution of the bromoalkane.
